text: Form NR74 Determination of Residency Status When Entering Canada. If you are unsure whether you are a Canadian resident for tax purposes, you can ask the CRA for a formal non-binding opinion by completing Form NR74. This form is useful when your situation is complex — for example if you maintain significant ties in both Canada and another country, if you arrived on a temporary permit but plan to stay, or if you have a spouse who will join you later. To complete NR74 you provide details about your residential ties including your home in Canada, your spouse or dependants, your personal property, your employment situation, and your immigration status. The CRA reviews the form and provides a written opinion on whether you are considered a resident. This opinion is not legally binding but provides guidance and shows good faith compliance. Download it from canada.ca and mail it to your regional tax services office.

Form RC151 Apply for Benefits Before Filing Your First Tax Return. As a newcomer to Canada, you may be eligible for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and other credits before you file your first tax return. Form RC151 allows you to apply for these benefits as soon as you arrive without waiting until you file your first full return. To complete RC151 you provide your Social Insurance Number, your date of arrival, your marital status, and information about your family members. If you have children you should also complete Form RC66 at the same time. Submit RC151 to your regional CRA tax centre by mail. Once processed the CRA will begin issuing your quarterly benefit payments without waiting for your tax return. This is especially important if you arrive in Canada mid-year — it can mean receiving several hundred dollars in benefit payments you would otherwise miss. You will still need to file a tax return for the year you arrive to confirm your entitlements.

Form RC66 How to Apply for the Canada Child Benefit as a Newcomer. If you have children under 18 and have recently arrived in Canada, apply for the Canada Child Benefit as soon as possible using Form RC66. You do not need to wait until you file your tax return. Complete RC66 with your SIN and your spouse SIN, your date of arrival, your immigration status and document number, the names and birthdates of each child, and confirmation of who is primarily responsible for each child. Attach copies of your immigration documents such as your work permit, study permit, or permanent resident card. Also attach proof of each child such as a birth certificate. Mail the completed form and documents to your regional CRA office or submit through CRA My Account. Processing typically takes 8 weeks. Once approved payments begin on the 20th of each month.

Benefits Credits and Taxes for Newcomers Official CRA Guide 2025-2026. The CRA retired the printed Guide T4055 in January 2025 and replaced it with a comprehensive digital resource called Benefits Credits and Taxes for Newcomers available at canada.ca. Key benefits covered include the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit which replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026 and pays 25 percent more, Canada Child Benefit, Canada Workers Benefit, provincial and territorial benefits, and the Canada Dental Care Plan. The guide is available in English and French and links to information in over 20 other languages. You can also call the CRA newcomer enquiries line at 1-800-959-8281 for personalized help in English or French, or use a telephonic interpreter for other languages.

BC Family Benefit Monthly Payments for BC Families with Children. The BC Family Benefit is a tax-free monthly payment from the Government of British Columbia for families with children under 18 who are residents of BC. For the 2025-2026 benefit year, the maximum annual BC Family Benefit is approximately 2,188 dollars for the first child, 1,375 dollars for each additional child, plus a single-parent supplement of 500 dollars for eligible single-parent families. The benefit is income-tested and phases out at higher income levels. You do not apply separately — the CRA administers the BC Family Benefit on behalf of BC and calculates your entitlement when you file your tax return and indicate you are a BC resident. Payments are combined with the Canada Child Benefit into one monthly payment. If you are a newcomer to BC with children, apply for the Canada Child Benefit using Form RC66 as soon as you arrive and the BC Family Benefit will be automatically calculated.

Alberta Child and Family Benefit Quarterly Payments for Alberta Families. The Alberta Child and Family Benefit (ACFB) is a tax-free payment for lower and middle income families with children under 18 living in Alberta. For 2025-2026, the maximum annual ACFB is 1,529 dollars for families with one child, 2,293 dollars for two children, 2,972 dollars for three children, and up to 5,966 dollars for families with four or more children. The benefit has two components: the base component available to families earning under approximately 43,000 dollars annually, and the working component for families with employment income. The CRA administers the ACFB on behalf of Alberta. You do not apply separately — eligibility is determined when you file your tax return. Payments are made quarterly in February, May, August, and November.

Quebec Benefits and Taxes for Newcomers Key Programs 2025-2026. Quebec residents file two tax returns: a federal return with the CRA and a separate provincial return with Revenu Quebec (TP-1-V). Quebec has its own pension plan (QPP instead of CPP) and parental insurance plan (QPIP instead of federal EI for maternity). The Solidarity Tax Credit combines the QST credit, housing component, and northern component into one refundable credit paid monthly with maximum amounts exceeding 1,500 dollars annually depending on family situation. The Quebec Family Allowance provides payments for children under 18 with a maximum of approximately 2,800 dollars annually for a first child. In 2026, Revenu Quebec introduced a special 50 dollar grocery and energy payment for all Quebec households. To receive Quebec benefits you must file the provincial TP-1-V return with Revenu Quebec in addition to the federal return. Contact Revenu Quebec at 1-800-267-6299.

Disability Tax Credit For Newcomers with Disabilities or Disabled Family Members. The Disability Tax Credit (DTC) is a non-refundable federal tax credit that reduces the amount of income tax owed by eligible individuals with a severe and prolonged impairment in physical or mental functions. For 2025, the federal DTC amount is 9,872 dollars for adults and 11,460 dollars for children under 18. Even if you owe no tax, unused DTC amounts can be transferred to a supporting family member who does owe tax. To apply, a medical practitioner must complete Form T2201 (Disability Tax Credit Certificate) confirming the nature and duration of the impairment. Eligible impairments include vision, speaking, hearing, walking, feeding, dressing, and mental functions necessary for everyday life. The impairment must be severe and prolonged lasting at least 12 months. The DTC is also the gateway to the Registered Disability Savings Plan and the Child Disability Benefit additional CCB supplement.

Child Care Expense Deduction For Newcomer Families with Young Children. The child care expense deduction allows you to deduct eligible child care expenses from your income, directly reducing the amount of income you are taxed on. Eligible expenses include payments for daycare centres, nursery schools, day camps, boarding schools, caregivers in your home, and after-school programs. The maximum deductible amount per child per year is 8,000 dollars for children under 7, 5,000 dollars for children aged 7 to 16, and 11,000 dollars for children eligible for the Disability Tax Credit. Generally the lower-income spouse must claim the deduction. If both spouses earn income both must work or attend school to be eligible. You need receipts from child care providers including their SIN if they are an individual. Claim this deduction on Line 21400 of your T1 return. You cannot claim child care expenses for school tuition fees or medical care.

Charitable Donation Tax Credit How Giving Reduces Your Taxes in Canada. When you donate to a registered Canadian charity, you receive a federal tax credit. The federal credit rate is 15 percent on the first 200 dollars of donations and 29 percent on amounts over 200 dollars. Provincial credits are added on top — combined federal and provincial credits can return approximately 40 to 50 percent of your donation. Only donations to registered Canadian charities qualify — verify at canada.ca/charities-giving. Donations from your spouse or common-law partner can be combined on one return to maximize the credit. Donations can be carried forward up to five years. As a newcomer, donations to Canadian charities qualify — donations to foreign charities generally do not qualify for the Canadian credit. Religious organizations registered with the CRA also qualify for donation receipts.

Home Accessibility Tax Credit For Seniors and Persons with Disabilities. The Home Accessibility Tax Credit (HATC) provides a 15 percent non-refundable federal tax credit on up to 20,000 dollars of eligible home renovation expenses per year — a maximum credit of 3,000 dollars. The HATC is available for renovations that make a home more accessible for a qualifying individual who is 65 or older at year-end, or an individual eligible for the Disability Tax Credit. Qualifying relatives who own or rent a home for a qualifying individual can also claim the credit. Eligible expenses include grab bars and handrails, wheelchair ramps or lifts, widening doorways for wheelchair access, walk-in bathtubs or showers, lowering countertops, and installing non-slip flooring. Landscaping, maintenance, and cosmetic improvements do not qualify. You need receipts from licensed contractors.

Canada Caregiver Credit For Newcomers Supporting Dependent Family Members. The Canada Caregiver Credit (CCC) is a non-refundable tax credit for individuals who support a spouse, common-law partner, or dependent with a physical or mental impairment. For 2025, the maximum CCC amount is 7,999 dollars for a spouse or common-law partner with an impairment, or 2,616 dollars for other dependants such as a parent, grandparent, child, or sibling. The credit is reduced dollar-for-dollar once the dependant net income exceeds 18,783 dollars in 2025. As a newcomer who has brought family members to Canada who have physical or mental impairments, you may qualify for this credit. You do not need a formal Disability Tax Credit approval to claim the CCC — a medical professional can certify the impairment. If your dependent family member has a very low income and lives with you, the Eligible Dependant Credit of up to 15,705 dollars may also apply.

Employment Expenses Newcomers Can Deduct Beyond the T4. Several employment-related expenses can be deducted if your employer requires you to pay them as a condition of employment. Your employer must complete Form T2200 to confirm each expense. Deductible employment expenses include union dues and professional membership fees shown on your T4 in Box 44 which are automatically deductible without T2200. Annual professional dues required by your profession such as engineering nursing or accounting association fees. Tools required by a tradesperson — the maximum deduction for 2025 is 500 dollars. Home office expenses if your employer requires you to work from home — deduct electricity, heat, internet, home insurance, and maintenance proportional to work space. Vehicle expenses if you use your personal vehicle for work travel (not commuting) — keep a mileage log. Legal fees paid to collect wages owed by an employer are also deductible. Claim employment expenses on Line 22900 using Form T777.

GST/HST Registration for Self-Employed Newcomers When and How. If you earn self-employment income in Canada and your total revenues exceed 30,000 dollars in any four consecutive calendar quarters, you are required to register for GST/HST and collect it from your clients. You must register within 29 days of exceeding the 30,000 dollar threshold. Register using Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number) online through the CRA Business Registration Online portal or by calling 1-800-959-5525. Once registered you receive a Business Number with a GST/HST account identifier. You must collect GST of 5 percent or HST which varies by province — Ontario is 13 percent, Nova Scotia 15 percent, BC is 12 percent — from clients, file GST/HST returns quarterly or annually, and remit the net tax to the CRA. The Quick Method is a simplified way to calculate GST/HST for service businesses with revenues under 400,000 dollars — you remit a lower percentage and keep the difference.

Quarterly Tax Instalments What They Are and When You Need Them. If you have income that does not have tax withheld at source such as self-employment income, rental income, or investment income, you may need to make quarterly tax instalment payments. The CRA requires instalments if your net tax owing is more than 3,000 dollars in the current year AND was more than 3,000 dollars in either of the two previous years. Instalments are due on March 15, June 15, September 15, and December 15 each year. The CRA sends instalment reminders with suggested payment amounts. You can pay using your bank online bill payment to CRA or through CRA My Account. As a newcomer in your first year of self-employment you typically do not need instalments until your second year — but it is smart to set aside 25 to 30 percent of self-employment income quarterly for taxes.

Investment Income for Newcomers T5 Slips and What to Report. If you have money in Canadian bank accounts or investments, you may receive investment income that must be reported. T5 (Statement of Investment Income) slips are issued by banks and investment firms by the end of February and report interest income from savings accounts and GICs, Canadian eligible dividends, Canadian non-eligible dividends, and foreign income. Interest income is fully taxable at your marginal rate. Eligible dividends from Canadian corporations receive a dividend tax credit — the effective tax rate is approximately 9 to 15 percent for most income levels. Foreign investment income must also be reported — convert to Canadian dollars and claim a foreign tax credit if you paid tax abroad. Interest earned inside a TFSA or RRSP is NOT reported — it grows tax-sheltered. Report investment income on Schedule 4 of your T1 return.

Common Tax Mistakes Newcomers Make in Canada. Mistake 1: Not filing because you think you owe money. Filing activates benefits worth hundreds of dollars annually even when you owe nothing. Mistake 2: Forgetting to report worldwide income earned after your arrival date in Canada. Mistake 3: Not accumulating TFSA room from arrival — your room starts from the year you arrive as a resident. Mistake 4: Not keeping receipts for medical expenses — the credit only applies to amounts above 3 percent of net income. Mistake 5: Not applying for the Canada Child Benefit immediately on arrival using Form RC66. Mistake 6: Using foreign income before arrival to calculate RRSP room — only Canadian income creates RRSP room. Mistake 7: Not filing Form T1135 for foreign property over 100,000 dollars — penalties start at 2,500 dollars minimum. Mistake 8: Not setting up direct deposit with the CRA — refunds and benefits take much longer by cheque. Mistake 9: Missing the RRSP contribution deadline of March 1 for the previous tax year.

How Tax Refunds Work in Canada What to Expect as a Newcomer. A tax refund occurs when income tax withheld from your pay (shown in Box 22 of your T4) exceeds your actual tax liability calculated on your return. This is common for newcomers who worked only part of the year after arriving, earned modest income and qualify for credits that reduce their tax below what was withheld, or are entitled to refundable credits. The CRA processes returns electronically filed through NETFILE within 2 weeks. Paper returns take up to 8 weeks. After processing the CRA issues a Notice of Assessment confirming the refund amount. With direct deposit your refund arrives in your bank account 5 to 10 business days after the NOA date. Without direct deposit the CRA mails a cheque which takes 2 to 8 additional weeks. As a newcomer who worked only half the year, your refund may be larger than average because standard withholding assumes a full year of income.

Non-Resident Withholding Tax For Newcomers Receiving Canadian Income Before Arriving. Non-resident withholding tax of 25 percent (or lower under a tax treaty) applies to Canadian dividends, rental income from Canadian property, Canadian pension payments, RRSP withdrawals, and certain other income paid to non-residents. Employment income earned in Canada by a non-resident is subject to regular payroll withholding. If you were a non-resident who received Canadian income with 25 percent withholding and then became a resident during the same year, you may be able to file a tax return and recover some of the excess withholding. NR4 slips report the amount of Canadian income paid to non-residents and the withholding tax deducted. As a newcomer who owned Canadian investments or rental property before arriving, notify your bank and investment firm of your new residency status to avoid incorrect withholding.

Departure Return If You Leave Canada After Being a Resident. If you leave Canada and cease to be a Canadian resident, you must file a special departure return for the year you left covering January 1 to your date of departure. On the date you cease to be a Canadian resident, you are deemed to have disposed of most of your property at fair market value — called a deemed disposition. Any accrued capital gains on investments or other assets trigger tax on departure. Exceptions include Canadian real estate, Canadian business property, and pension rights which remain taxable in Canada. You must report all income earned in Canada up to your departure date. Credits and deductions are prorated based on the fraction of the year you were a resident. File your departure return by April 30 of the following year. Include Schedule T when you have property subject to deemed disposition.

Tuition Tax Credit Complete Guide for International Students and Newcomers. The tuition tax credit reduces your federal tax by 15 percent of eligible tuition fees paid to a qualifying Canadian educational institution including universities, colleges, and CEGEPs. Eligible fees include tuition fees, application fees if you register and attend, and examination fees. Not eligible: student association fees, housing costs, meal plans, and health insurance premiums. Your school provides a T2202 (Tuition and Enrolment Certificate) by February 28 showing eligible fees. Enter T2202 information on Schedule 11 of your T1 return. If the tuition credit exceeds your tax owing, you can carry forward the unused amount to a future year indefinitely, or transfer up to 5,000 dollars of unused credits to a spouse, common-law partner, parent, or grandparent who is a Canadian resident. For international students who pay higher international tuition rates, the full international tuition fee is eligible.

Ontario Trillium Benefit 2025-2026 Amounts and How to Claim. The Ontario Trillium Benefit (OTB) combines three provincial credits into one monthly payment: the Ontario Sales Tax Credit, the Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit, and the Northern Ontario Energy Credit. For the July 2025 to June 2026 benefit year, the maximum Ontario Sales Tax Credit is 371 dollars per adult and 371 dollars per child. The maximum Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit is 1,248 dollars for non-seniors and 1,421 dollars for those 65 and older. Renters claim the property tax equivalent of rent paid — the formula considers 20 percent of rent paid as a property tax equivalent. Homeowners claim actual property taxes paid. To claim the OTB complete the ON-BEN form when you file your Ontario T1 return. If your total annual benefit is 360 dollars or less you receive it in one July payment. If over 360 dollars you receive monthly payments beginning in July.

Northern Residents Deduction For Newcomers Living in Remote Areas. If you live in a prescribed northern or intermediate zone for at least six consecutive months during the year, you can claim the Northern Residents Deduction. Prescribed northern zones include the Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut, northern Quebec, northern Ontario, Labrador, and many remote communities across Canada. The deduction has two parts: a residency deduction of 11 dollars per day for Zone A or 5.50 dollars per day for Zone B for each day you lived in the zone, and a travel deduction for the lowest return airfare to the nearest major city if you received a taxable travel benefit from your employer. The deduction is claimed on Line 25500 using Form T2222. As a newcomer who accepts work in a northern or remote community in industries like mining, oil and gas, healthcare, or education, this deduction can significantly reduce your Canadian tax.

Non-Refundable Tax Credits Complete List for Newcomers 2025-2026. Non-refundable tax credits reduce your federal tax payable but cannot create a refund on their own. Key credits for newcomers include: Basic Personal Amount of 16,129 dollars for 2025 and 16,452 dollars for 2026 — everyone gets this. Spousal Amount if your spouse earned less than 16,129 dollars. Eligible Dependant Amount if you support a child who lives with you. Canada Caregiver Credit for supporting a dependant with an impairment. CPP Contributions Credit — 15 percent federal credit on your CPP contributions from Box 16 of T4. EI Premiums Credit — 15 percent credit on EI premiums from Box 18 of T4. Canada Employment Amount of up to 1,433 dollars for 2025 for any employment income. Tuition Amount of 15 percent credit on eligible tuition from T2202. Medical Expenses of 15 percent on expenses over 3 percent of net income or 2,759 dollars. Charitable Donations of 15 percent on first 200 dollars and 29 percent on the rest. Disability Amount for you or a dependant with a certified severe impairment.

Social Insurance Number and Individual Tax Number Which One Do You Need. A Social Insurance Number (SIN) is required to work in Canada and to access government programs. Apply at Service Canada in person with your immigration documents. If you have authorization to work through a work permit, study permit with work authorization, or permanent residence, you qualify for a SIN. A SIN beginning with 9 indicates a temporary resident and is valid while your immigration status is valid. If you do not have authorization to work in Canada and are not eligible for a SIN, you may need an Individual Tax Number (ITN). An ITN is a 9-digit number the CRA assigns for tax purposes only. Apply for an ITN using Form T1261 (Application for a Canada Revenue Agency Individual Tax Number for Non-Residents). ITNs are typically used by international students without work authorization who have investment income, and non-residents selling Canadian property. If you later receive work authorization and become eligible for a SIN, apply for a SIN and inform the CRA to link your ITN to your new SIN.

Registered Disability Savings Plan RDSP for Newcomers with Disabilities. The Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) is a long-term savings plan for Canadians with disabilities and their families. To open an RDSP the beneficiary must be a Canadian resident under age 60, have a valid SIN, and be approved for the Disability Tax Credit. The federal government provides two types of grants: the Canada Disability Savings Grant which matches contributions up to 300 percent depending on income, and the Canada Disability Savings Bond which provides up to 1,000 dollars per year to low-income holders with no contribution required. Contributions to an RDSP are not tax-deductible but all investment growth is tax-sheltered. Withdrawals are partially taxed in the hands of the beneficiary. There is a 10-year holdback rule — if you withdraw money within 10 years of receiving a grant or bond, you must repay the grants. Open an RDSP at most Canadian banks and credit unions.
